text: CI and test speed was a huge blocker; the suite was huge, bloated and unoptimized
Much of the test suite enforced what should have been compile-time or type-level facts
The full suite ran on unrelated changes; a small data change forced a full rebuild and recheck
App code and trip data were not separated (not a general travel app taking data files)
Nobody knew which code affected which features, so everything was rechecked and CI ran out
Development was serial: the current feature blocked unrelated work (worst with #72)
Criticality was haphazard and miscalibrated in both directions, with no triage across the spec
Tracking implemented versus unimplemented features was a mess
Worktrees did not share a compiler cache or build directory
Simulators were shared instead of one per agent or test group
Flaky tests were retried and forgotten instead of flagged and fixed
The UI check used a browser for facts that need no layout, and for untouched screens
Data was keyed by leg numbers, not stable ids; generated files were large and coarse
Most time was spent waiting for CI and tests
The main session relayed every hand-off while agents sat idle
No single source of truth: status files, a handoff note and the main session's context
Agents collided on simulators, Chrome, search quota and data files
Ownership of work was unclear
Work died with the session or the laptop
Exists plus green CI was taken to mean correct
How data was verified (simulator, user, online sources) was tribal knowledge, not typed
The spec was not encoded; the code was its own definition of done
Manual steps (simulator runs, Playwright lookups) were never proceduralized and left no trail
Tests that cannot fail were counted as evidence
Performance profiles and optimisation effort were not recorded
Push after every commit was a written rule; the overnight fixer pushed only once at the end
The owner reviews and merges every PR, a bottleneck that worsens as agents parallelise; goal: most PRs merged sight-unseen, with merge authority earned per risk tier
The owner does triage, priority and wall-time watching by hand; goal: a steward role reads the log, flags budget trends and blocking work, escalates only decisions
source: docs/SPEC.md Goal: automate the owner's triage/priority/wall-time role

DISCUSS: CI watcher Stop semantics for timed-out and absent pushes. Now: timed-out (1h) and absent (no run by timeout; interim absent after appear_millis) let Stop pass; unavailable (every job in every run failed with no steps) lets Stop pass; ci-wait exits non-zero for all but passed. Fail closed forever would block a stuck agent with no exit but the owner; failing open waives CI for silent stalls. Agent wall-time budgets (30-60 min) are shorter than the 1h timeout, so a stalled run outlives the agent either way. Unavailable is inferred from job shape only; a billing/spending-limit annotation (gh api check-runs/<job>/annotations) would make it certain at the cost of one call per job. Owner's call.

Found adopting in Basho (507 findings from lints Basho did not run). Options: treat a missing prior policy as first adoption, or an explicit owner-approved raise.

DISCUSS: test-time has no place for a slow integration test. Basho's UI check (headless Chrome over every screen) takes ~260 s as one test; with millis.per_test=1000/total=4000 test-time fails and cannot be baselined. It also reruns every test one by one after the test step, so Basho's ci doubles from ~4.5 to ~9 min. Options: per-test or per-crate allowances in policy, exclude a named test set, or reuse timings from the test step.

Unprimed review found 4 regressions with one root cause: a background or parallel push is missed, so Stop passes on failed CI; another worktree's push is counted as this session's; a reviewer's git pull of a red branch blocks Stop forever; a read-only .git blocks every Stop. meta gc: a cleanup chore run on a schedule and at session start. Remove agent worktrees and clones whose branch is merged or closed and whose task is not claimed; delete target dirs untouched for a day; clear finished scratch clones; never touch work that is unpushed, uncommitted, or in use. Report what it freed. It decides from tracked state (tasks, claims, PR states, agents), so it shares a source with the monitoring of open tickets and agents.

meta status: one live view of open tasks and their claims, each task's PR and CI state, and each agent's worktree, process and last activity (agents log their worktree when they claim). Flags anything that isn't green and ready, actively worked, or owner-blocked. It is the shared source for the steward heartbeat (stalled work) and for meta gc (disk).

meta rm <path>...: the only way agents delete files. Deletes only (1) a cargo target dir, or (2) a git worktree or clone whose work is all on a remote: no uncommitted, untracked or stashed changes; every local branch and HEAD on a remote branch; no ignored files other than target dirs. Worktrees go through git worktree remove. Refuses anything in use (an open file or a process cwd inside it). Logs what it removed and the space freed. It becomes the deletion layer of meta gc.

Agents run commands the harness flags for approval (rm, python or heredoc rewrites of tracked files), which stalls them until the owner answers. Rule: agents never do anything the harness flags. Enforce in the PreToolUse hook: block known flag patterns with a message naming the safe alternative (Edit tool, git checkout, meta rm), so the agent corrects itself instead of waiting.

Budget as a typed entity (agreed with owner 2026-10-26): units Count, Duration, Share, maybe Money or CI minutes, one unit per budget; windows per change (ratchet against the merge base), rolling per period, or standing; the overspend action is part of each budget's definition (block by default, or escalate to DISCUSS); spend recorded by measurement only (CI and tools), with severity as the judged exception checked by calibration; definitions stay in policy.toml as typed entries with ids, and spend events in the log point at them; raising a budget is owner-only.

Divisions (agreed with owner 2026-10-26): a division is any behaviour or invariant made first class; divisions nest arbitrarily, and each child gets a subset of its parent's budget. Top level per project: (1) feature development and maintenance (for example navigation); (2) performance and cost (CI performance included); (3) architecture and planning, which feeds 1 and 2. Each top-level division has its own status tracking and metrics, and controls its own soundness, testing and measurability. Every item belongs to exactly one division; meta status, budgets and severity are per division; an agent sees only its division's context.

Severity and divisions (agreed with owner 2026-10-26): each division owns its severity scale, including nested divisions, and deeper divisions have finer scales; caps are split down the tree. Waivers spend from the budget of the division whose rule they bend. The ladder sits in architecture and planning, which types concerns into divisions. meta status is a tree of divisions, each with its own metrics. meta-dev is an ordinary project with the same three top-level divisions; the steward and triage sit in its architecture and planning division.

Spec rules as typed records (build step 0, agreed with owner 2026-10-26): each spec rule is a typed entry with id, division, wording, rung and enforcer (a type, lint, test or CI step); SPEC.md becomes a rendered view; a lint checks every named enforcer exists, and that a rung-4 claim points at a type; mutation testing proves enforcers bite; unattached prose counts against the vagueness budget, which only goes down; architecture and planning status reports the share of rules per rung.
